title: Tube-Based Robust Data-Driven Predictive Control for Linear Parameter-Varying Systems With Noisy Data
summary: This paper proposes a tube-based robust data-driven predictive control scheme for unknown discrete-time linear parameter-varying (LPV) systems using offline noisy input-scheduling-state data. We establish a multi-trajectory simplified LPV fundamental lemma yielding a collective Hankel representation of finite-horizon trajectories. Constraining the Hankel coefficients to a scaled simplex uniformly bounds the noise-induced predictor mismatch but may exclude relevant constrained lifted trajectories. A convex-hull coverage condition for admissible receding-horizon continuations restores the required representability. LPV data-consistency and robust positively invariant sets provide tube-tightening ingredients computed directly from noisy data. The online problem is a quadratic program, for which recursive feasibility, closed-loop constraint satisfaction, and practical input-to-state stability are established. Numerical results illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed scheme.

title: Heterogeneous Risk-Sensitive Evolutionary Learning in Coordination Games: Polarization, Welfare Loss, and Intervention for Efficiency
summary: We study evolutionary learning in coordination games in a finite population of agents with heterogeneous risk attitudes, modeled using the entropic risk measure (ERM). The population consists of two subpopulations, each with a fixed risk attitude. Under risk-sensitive best response with mutations (BRM), we characterize the long-run outcomes of the learning process. In particular, we characterize when a polarized state, in which the two subpopulations choose different actions, is uniquely stochastically stable in terms of agents' risk attitudes and the subpopulation sizes. Notably, this polarized state is strictly Pareto dominated by the payoff-dominant equilibrium under both expected payoffs and agents' own ERM-adjusted payoffs. Moreover, its welfare, measured by average expected payoff, is always lower than that of the payoff-dominant equilibrium and can also be lower than that of the risk-dominant equilibrium. Thus, heterogeneity of risk attitudes in learning alone can lead to an inefficient long-run outcome. To mitigate such inefficiency, we propose intervention mechanisms to modify agents' risk attitudes in learning. We show that a sufficiently large intervention share (the fraction of agents modified) and sufficiently high intervention intensity (the increase in their risk parameter) ensure that the payoff-dominant equilibrium is uniquely stochastically stable. However, greater intervention intensity cannot compensate for an insufficient intervention share, and a larger intervention share cannot compensate for insufficient intervention intensity.

title: Adaptive Robust Optimisation for Frequency-Constrained Market Clearing Problem
summary: This paper formulates the day-ahead market clearing as a two-stage adaptive robust optimisation problem in which the first stage determines unit commitment, energy dispatch, and reserve procurement, while the second stage represents worst-case balancing actions under simultaneous uncertainty in renewable generation, load, and HVDC converter outages. Frequency security is enforced explicitly through inertia and fast frequency response constraints at the synchronous-area level, with HVDC lines allowed to provide emergency power support within their available headroom. The resulting min--max--min problem is solved by a column-and-constraint generation algorithm and applied to an eight-country North Sea test system comprising three synchronous areas, sixteen onshore bidding zones, and five offshore wind farm hubs connected through a meshed HVDC grid. We compare the Home Market (HM) and Offshore Bidding Zone (OBZ) designs on this infrastructure across different uncertainty scenarios. The results first demonstrate the value of robustness, where deterministic solutions that ignore uncertainty are severely vulnerable to worst-case realisations. Comparing the two designs, we find that OBZ's offshore zone boundaries make line congestion visible to the day-ahead market, enabling targeted reserve procurement that raises day-ahead costs but substantially reduces real-time load shedding, yielding a net reduction in total system cost that grows with the severity of localised offshore uncertainty. When both designs face the identical worst-case contingency, HM cannot distinguish an offshore converter trip from normal operation and thus fails to hedge against it, while OBZ considers the risk at the day-ahead stage. This advantage can be seasonal, scaling with the ratio of offshore wind output to HVDC line capacity and diminishing when onshore generation dominates the supply mix.

title: Your bids are showing: re-identifying power plants in anonymized market data, and a differentially private alternative
summary: ERCOT publishes every generator's hourly offer curve 60 days after the operating day. Market monitors, researchers and traders use these records to study the merit order and check for withholding. PJM publishes the same kind of data with unit names replaced by codes, on the view that masking keeps offers confidential. We test that view on ERCOT data from 2024 to 2026, where names are public and so provide ground truth, by masking the records under PJM's published rules. Public EIA and EPA data match 25% of the masked units we can score (32% of their capacity) to their plant, and 45% fall within the top five guesses. PJM's feed carries the same fields, so we expect masking to fail there too. Publishing exact fuel-group totals instead does not help. An attacker who knows the other units in a group recovers one unit's high-price offers exactly, and an outsider who knows only the target's outage dates reaches a correlation of 0.77, most of it from a few renewable and hydro units that offer at very high prices (0.32 over fossil units). We propose a differentially private release: monthly totals by fuel group and price bin, with Gaussian noise calibrated under zero-concentrated differential privacy so that each unit's whole year of offers is protected. It publishes an unbiased noisy layer and derives a monotone supply curve and shares from it at no extra privacy cost. At $\varepsilon=10$ per unit-year the market supply curve stays within 11% of the truth, the implied clearing price within \$3.0/MWh, and the attacker's correlation falls to 0.23. Whether an analysis still works depends on one ratio, how much the true quantity varies month to month against the noise, which predicts the accuracy of totals to within 0.05. The clearing price, supply slope and combined-cycle capacity remain usable, but no monthly release, private or exact, can answer questions about single hours or single units.

title: Automated classification of modal displacements
summary: The bending, torsional, or coupled character of a mode shape helps determine the dynamic behaviour of aerospace and civil structures. In vibration testing, it is assigned by inspecting mode shape plots, and depends on the analyst. This work proposes four indices to describe the motion of a mode from a few sensor vectors: a bending score, a torsion score, a twist share and an in-plane ratio. They are assessed on the first eight finite element modes of a tapered plate with a swept trailing edge. They are applied to identified XB-2 wing modes and to the published modes of the Sheraton Universal Hotel, a reinforced concrete (RC) building. On the plate, the twist share separates bending, coupled and torsion modes. The XB-2 modes include one bending and three coupled modes (one dominated by in-plane bending and two by out-of-plane bending). The coupled mode dominated by in-plane bending (15.25 Hz, in-plane ratio 1.33) was not investigated in earlier campaigns on the wing. On the RC building, all five modes are bending (twist share below 0.0005). The twist share and the in-plane ratio indicate the type of each mode. Hence, modes are classified without visually inspecting the mode shapes. Code and processed data are openly released.

title: One Release for All: Private Simple Linear Regression Via Improved Simplex Mapping
summary: We present a single-release extension of DP-RSS for private simple linear regression when both input and output are bounded in $[0,1]$. Rather than privately releasing several related sufficient-statistic estimates, we encode the required information in one unit-sensitivity vector and apply the Laplace mechanism once at the full privacy budget. The required least-squares sufficient statistics are then recovered by deterministic post-processing and used directly in an ordinary least-squares solve. We obtain variance reductions of $1.67$--$2.67\times$ relative to DP-RSS for several statistics. Experiments show that the benefit is most pronounced in the high-privacy regime, while the methods converge as privacy noise becomes negligible.

title: When Coupling Backfires: BBR-Induced L4S Degradation under DualPI2
comment: Accepted to the IEEE Consumer Communications & Networking Conference (CCNC), LATENCY Workshop, 2027
summary: Low Latency, Low Loss, Scalable Throughput (L4S) uses DualPI2 to separate low latency (e.g., TCP Prague) and Classic flows into two queues while coupling their congestion signals. However, this coupling is designed for Reno-like Classic congestion controls, while widely deployed BBR behaves differently. Prior studies observed severe Prague throughput degradation when BBR occupies the Classic queue under DualPI2, but the mechanism remains insufficiently explained. Through controlled testbed experiments and an extension of an existing BBRv1/BBRv2 fluid model with PI2, we show that BBR can drive the PI2 base probability p' far above CUBIC levels, producing strong coupled marking that can nearly starve Prague despite low L4S queueing delay. The model explains BBRv1's persistent high-p' regime, BBRv2's lower, oscillating p', and their dependence on the PI2 target relative to RTT. Additional experiments show that Prague throughput degradation also occurs with BBRv3. Our findings highlight the need for coupling mechanisms supporting low latency flows across heterogeneous Classic congestion controls.

title: The Industrialization of Noise: Why Automated Proof-Solving is the Same Old Dead End
summary:
Nearly fifty years ago, DeMillo, Lipton, and Perlis argued that mathematical proofs are not static, isolated structures of formal logic, but the products of a vibrant, evolving social process of human critique, internalization, and shared intuition. In October 2026, OpenAI challenged this thesis by releasing a massive repository of 722 automated mathematical manuscripts, claiming full or partial solutions to 372 longstanding open problems. This paper examines the immediate crisis through the lens of the original DLP framework. We argue that the sudden, automated overproduction of dense, unreadable proofs represents an industrial pollution of the mathematical ecosystem. By examining the three fatal structural pillars of this automated approach (Specification, Regress, and Utility), we demonstrate that decoupling the act of mechanical solving from the human social process of understanding produces a sterile repository of dead logical artifacts.
  The resulting industrialization of unexamined manuscripts is self-fulfilling. Flooding the literature guarantees that the finite supply of human attention will lose the race to separate signal from noise. In this sense, posting a result is not the same act as submitting it to the community processes by which mathematics is vetted, digested, and incorporated into shared knowledge.

title: Local subspace encoding for spectral prediction: from TabPFN to operator-adaptive calibration
comment: 25 pages, 10 figures (including 3 supplementary figures). Evidence bundle: https://github.com/GBeurier/nirs4all-aom/releases/tag/lvse-gcu-evidence-v1
summary: TabPFN has already shown useful predictive performance on near-infrared spectra. RamanPFN subsequently proposed two spectral representations for tabular inference: Global Compositional Unmixing (GCU) and Local Vibrational Subspace Encoding (LVSE). We assess whether these representations also help on datasets assembled through the nirs4all ecosystem, and whether their value extends to classical calibration. We reanalyse completed experiments from a public spectral dataset catalogue. On a post-hoc subset of 61 matched numerical prediction tasks, after excluding ten class-code, metadata or semantically ambiguous targets, LVSE reduces RMSE relative to raw-spectrum TabPFN by 10.22%, 12.80% and 14.52% on average for checkpoints 2.5, 3 and 3.5, respectively, with median reductions of 4.99%, 4.74% and 7.82%. Across 76 classification datasets, weighted F1 increases by 2.22, 2.56 and 3.81 percentage points. The 2.5 classification procedure uses output coding on 15 datasets exceeding the checkpoint's native class limit. GCU alone is less reliable in this implementation. LVSE also improves PLS and Ridge in many cases, with median RMSE reductions of 4.75% and 1.89%. Adding LVSE candidates to an operator-adaptive model is feasible, but a separate 35-task panel derived from the public AOM benchmark shows only small median gains. These results motivate evaluating LVSE alongside existing representation choices. They do not establish that a selector choosing between raw and LVSE inputs will improve every task.

title: Gaussian Process Data-Driven Hamiltonian for Probabilistic Safe Set Construction
comment: 16 pages, 4 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to the 9th Annual Learning for Dynamics and Control Conference (L4DC 2027)
summary: Hamilton-Jacobi (HJ) reachability is a general framework for verifying the safety of nonlinear systems, but it relies on an accurate dynamics model. The data-driven Hamiltonian (DDH) framework avoids system identification by lower-bounding the Hamiltonian directly from state-control-velocity data. However, it requires a Lipschitz bound on the unknown dynamics which is hard to certify from finite data, and as a single global constant this bound makes the computed safe sets conservative. We propose the Gaussian process data-driven Hamiltonian (GP-DDH), a fully data-driven framework that constructs safe sets with probabilistic guarantees under a GP prior on the dynamics. Furthermore, we suggest two methods to choose the confidence parameter $β$, both mathematically guaranteed to underbound the Hamiltonian. The computed safe set lies inside the true one with posterior probability at least $1-Δ$ for any $Δ\in(0,1)$. Numerical experiments show that GP-DDH recovers a bigger volume of the true safe set than DDH while still correctly providing a conservative approximation, even when DDH is given a Lipschitz constant computed from the true dynamics.

title: A concave-convex approach to bit depth allocation for linear MMSE estimation in wireless sensor networks with correlated noise
summary: Nodes in a wireless sensor network (WSN) are generally powered by batteries, and therefore energy efficiency is crucial. The bit depth used to quantize the sensor signal samples heavily influences energy consumption, as it strongly impacts the amount of information to be transmitted between the sensor nodes. Bit depth allocation problems seek to assign a bit depth to each sensor signal to optimize network resources, such as energy or bandwidth, together with algorithmic performance. We study a general bit depth allocation problem for linear minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimation in WSNs with spatially correlated noise and a communication energy model depending linearly on the sensor bit depths. This model follows from common configurations in digital communications with orthogonal multiple-access schemes. After relaxation to real variables, we formulate the resulting non-convex problem as a difference of convex (DC) problem, and develop an algorithm based on the concave-convex procedure (CCP) to find a local optimum. We show that the convex problem involved in each CCP iteration can be efficiently solved with a worst-case complexity that is linear in the number of sensors. Additionally, we show that our approach is more computationally efficient than previously proposed bit depth allocation algorithms and generic optimization methods, and it achieves significant energy savings.

title: Single-Photon Detectors for Optical Wireless Communications: A Tutorial
summary: Photon-counting receivers extend optical wireless communication (OWC) into regimes in which only a few detected photons are available per information bit, but the detector can no longer be treated as an interchangeable ideal counter. This tutorial develops a communication-oriented, port-to-bit framework for single-photon detection in indoor, terrestrial, airborne, space, underwater, non-line-of-sight, and integrated communication-and-sensing links. It compares SPADs, silicon photomultipliers, CMOS SPAD arrays, superconducting nanowire single-photon detectors, PMT/MCP-PMT receivers, upconversion detectors, and emerging technologies through photon-detection efficiency, timing, active area, dynamic range, spectral coverage, readout, cooling, and integration requirements. Beginning with the ideal Poisson channel, the tutorial then develops communication-level models for dead time, recovery, finite-pixel occupancy, saturation, background counts, afterpulsing, crosstalk, nonuniformity, and event loss. These models are connected to modulation, likelihood-based detection, synchronization, channel estimation, soft decoding, and detector-aware receiver processing, with numerical studies that compare algorithms under a common detector and detectors under a common algorithm. Finally, a unified link-budget and system co-design methodology is used to relate photons per bit, sensitivity, bandwidth, data rate, and link margin, and representative demonstrations are normalized to expose practical tradeoffs. The central conclusion is that useful photon efficiency is an end-to-end property of the optical front end, detector, readout, and digital receiver, rather than a detector metric in isolation.

title: Inference-Aware Congestion Control for Distributed MoE Inference
summary: Congestion control is central to low-latency datacenter communication, yet link utilization and queue state do not reveal whether delivered bytes advance an application. This distinction matters in distributed mixture-of-experts (MoE) inference: collective transfers jointly satisfy GPU dependencies, while computation may overlap with communication. The transfer limiting a consumer can therefore change over time, and extra bandwidth may have little effect while that consumer is still computing. We study this interaction and present IACC, which combines ACK/INT feedback with collective and consumer progress when allocating QP rates. A fixed-snapshot analysis characterizes budget conservation and weighted max-min allocation. Across five trace-guided workloads at baseline arrival density, IACC lowers mean TTFT and TPOT relative to HPCC by 6.32%-19.41% and 7.02%-27.33%, respectively. Across tested workload-density settings through 1.25x, mean and p95 TTFT are also lower.

title: Information Security Risk Preparedness in Electronic Data Interchange: A Comparative Assessment of General IT and Healthcare Environments
summary: Electronic Data Interchange (EDI) supports the exchange of structured information across business and healthcare environments, making information security and organizational risk management critical to reliable digital transactions. This study empirically assesses security-control preparedness and organizational risk-taking ability in EDI-related environments through a comparative analysis of General IT Professionals (GIT) and Healthcare EDI Professionals (HEP). A quantitative, cross-sectional survey was conducted with 100 respondents, equally divided between the two groups. Security Control Preparedness (SCP) and Threat Perception (TP) were validated using reliability and exploratory factor analyses, followed by group comparisons, correlation analysis, and multiple linear regression. HEP respondents reported significantly higher SCP than GIT respondents (M = 4.70 vs. 3.89, p < 0.001, d = 1.06) and higher Organizational Risk-Taking Ability (ORTA) (M = 6.14 vs. 5.28, p = 0.001, d = 0.66). In contrast, GIT respondents reported higher threat perception (M = 2.95 vs. 2.04, p < 0.001, d = 0.72). SCP was positively associated with ORTA (r = 0.479, p < 0.001), whereas TP showed a significant negative association (r = -0.610, p < 0.001). A parsimonious regression model incorporating SCP and TP explained 41.6% of the variance in ORTA (R^2 = 0.416, adjusted R^2 = 0.404, p < 0.001). Based on these empirical findings, an EDI Risk Management Framework (EDI-RMF) is proposed integrating governance, human and organizational security, technical safeguards, physical protection, and continuous monitoring. The findings provide empirical evidence for strengthening information-security risk management in EDI-enabled environments, particularly within developing-economy contexts.

title: Actionwave: A Systematic Benchmark for Waveform-Centric Clinical Prediction Across Care Scenarios
summary: Continuous bedside waveforms record rapid physiological changes that can inform clinical decisions. Existing benchmarks examine selected prediction conditions, but it remains unclear how model advantages depend on signal duration, warning time, and available inputs across care settings. We introduce Actionwave, a benchmark for waveform-centric clinical prediction across intensive-care, operating-room, and emergency-department settings. Actionwave uses a common decision-time prediction interface and groups clinically grounded tasks by what is inferred and when. It varies conditions relevant to clinical use, including the warning required before an intervention. We compare diverse architectures and pretrained biosignal encoders under specified model-size and compute budgets. The protocol requires patient-level splits, strict information cutoffs, and comparisons that isolate individual modeling factors. Across 20 tasks and 1.4M task-labelled windows from source datasets, the experimental grids account for over 87,000 model fits. These comparisons identify task-specific choices and show why matched cohorts, unimodal controls, and explicit timing are necessary when interpreting waveform model performance.

title: Federated Policy Gradient for Dynamic Consensus: Gradient Dominance and Topological Bounds
summary: This paper presents a federated optimization framework for dynamic consensus in homogeneous multi-agent systems. The underlying problem is challenged by the communication graph's spectral properties, which induce spatial heterogeneity and complicate decentralized control even when the dynamics of the agents are completely known. The problem is addressed in this paper by bridging distributed control theory with federated policy gradients. Accordingly, a comprehensive optimization landscape for dynamic consensus is established through a modal decomposition formulation. Specifically, a parameterized suboptimality bound is characterized that explicitly decouples the true aggregate policy gradient from the network covariance mismatch. Building on this formulation, sufficient conditions based on the graph's Laplacian spectrum are derived to recover exact gradient dominance, which guarantees convergence to the global consensus policy and establishes a lower bound on the achievable dominance coefficient. Furthermore, a Federated model-free consensus algorithm is proposed that utilizes zeroth-order exploration alongside a bisection-based discount factor annealing mechanism, successfully eliminating the need for an initial stabilizing policy. This approach achieves linear global convergence for policy optimization subroutines while maintaining strictly bounded outer iterations until dynamic consensus is achieved. Through extensive simulation studies and comparative feasibility analyses across diverse network topologies, it is demonstrated that the proposed federated approach consistently outperforms existing model-based and data-driven separation-based techniques.

title: Modeling Lunar Power Harvesting and Battery Recharging In The Presence of Random Pointing Error
summary: In our work, we establish a lunar power beaming environment between a low-lunar orbiter and a circular solar panel mounted on top of a lunar vehicle located at the Lunar South Pole. Due to the random nature of the pointing errors, various upper bounds reflecting the severity of these errors are considered. Although harvested power is modelled stochastically in the literature, we extend this randomness to battery-storage analysis by deriving PDFs of state of charge, accumulated battery capacity and energy, and end-to-end efficiency for both battery charging modes. Then, our derivations are verified with extensive Monte Carlo simulations. Hence, our derivations provide a mathematical model that enables prediction and helps us understand the randomness of the corresponding variables. For the given pointing error levels, we quantify the differences between charging modes in these battery metrics. Our work explains the stochastic nature of these battery metrics in a realistic lunar environment. Regarding the end-to-end efficiency metric, which is the ratio of the stored electrical energy to the transmitted electrical energy, we observed that slow-charging efficiency is immune to pointing errors, and this mode can utilize only one-sixth of what the link can deliver under a mild pointing error.

title: Predictive Self-Entropy in Dirichlet Universal Coding: A Factor-Two Central Limit Theorem and a Markov Extension
summary: Sequential universal coders produce both a realized log-loss and, before each symbol is observed, a predictive distribution with its own Shannon entropy. We compare the realized arithmetic code length with the cumulative predictive self-entropy, the prequential sum of the self-expected logarithmic scores of the issued forecasts. This forecast-only quantity is neither a plug-in entropy estimate nor a posterior entropy functional. For finite-alphabet memoryless sources and Dirichlet (add-$α$) sequential predictors, we prove a joint central limit theorem for the two normalized quantities. They have the same first-order entropy limit but different second-order fluctuations: for every nonuniform i.i.d. source, cumulative predictive self-entropy has exactly twice the leading asymptotic variance of realized code length, and the ordinary mean-square-error ratio converges to two. We also give its logarithmic bias coefficient. For fixed finite-order Markov sources with context-wise Dirichlet predictors, the factor-two result becomes a context/innovation covariance decomposition, recovering the i.i.d. factor two when only the innovation component contributes.

title: Energy and Performance Characterization of UxNBs: Toward AI-Driven Non-Terrestrial Open RAN Control
summary: UAV-mounted base stations (UxNBs) can provide ondemand 5G coverage, but their limited onboard energy makes power consumption the main operational constraint. AI-driven Open RAN controllers are a promising solution, yet they are trained almost exclusively on analytical models and simulations, since no public dataset captures the real energy behavior of a flying 5G base station (BS). As a first step toward closing this gap, we present a UAV testbed hosting a 5G picocell that supports a 20 MHz carrier and up to 100 Mbps throughput. The testbed measures BS system metrics, including power consumption, CPU load, and temperature, alongside UAV flight telemetry and detailed per-layer vRAN processing metrics. To our knowledge, this is the first demonstration that jointly exposes the energy and RAN behavior of a flying 5G BS, providing the real measurements needed to train and validate energy-aware AI controllers.

title: Towards Efficient Attack Tree Generation from Attack Graphs for Unobservable Target Analysis
summary: Attack trees provide a structured approach to security analysis but traditionally require prior knowledge of the attacker's objective. In practice, this objective often remains hidden, even when some attacker actions are partially detected. This paper presents a methodology for generating attack trees without assuming a predefined target by modeling the threat environment as a constraint-weighted graph and applying temporal reachability analysis. The approach identifies probable attacker locations from partial observations and a time budget, carrying traversal cost as an attack-tree attribute. It then extracts target-oriented subgraphs that preserve feasible attack paths while eliminating irrelevant nodes. We demonstrate the framework across three scenarios: a single office building, a multi-building industrial complex, and a real IoT device-communication network recovered from the CICIoT2023 attack dataset. Compared with the baselines, our approach achieves a lower reduction factor while maintaining complete target preservation, substantially outperforming topology-only methods that ignore temporal constraints. We further perform a sensitivity analysis across 66 weight configurations, showing that target identification is stable when strategic value receives at least 20\% of the weight in the single building and at least 50\% in the multi-building complex, while additional experiments reveal sensitivity to perturbations of the underlying strategic-value prior.

title: Chain-of-Thought Is Not Explainability
comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Position Paper Track). 27 pages, 3 figures
summary: Chain-of-thought (CoT) allows language models to verbalise multi-step rationales before producing their final answer. While this technique often boosts task performance and offers an impression of transparency into the model's reasoning, this position paper argues that rationales generated by current CoT techniques can be misleading and are neither necessary nor sufficient for trustworthy interpretability. We analyse faithfulness as whether CoTs are not only human-interpretable but also reflect the model's underlying reasoning well enough to support responsible use. By synthesising evidence from prior work, we systematically show that verbalised chains are frequently unfaithful, diverging from the critical hidden computations that drive a model's predictions. As CoT is increasingly relied upon in application domains, including high-stakes ones such as medicine, law, and autonomous systems, we further argue that this unfaithfulness is not taken seriously enough in these settings: our analysis of 1,000 recent CoT-centric papers finds that approximately 21.7% explicitly treat CoT as a load-bearing interpretability technique, building pipelines or safety arguments that would not hold if CoT is unfaithful to the model's actual reasoning. They include papers in high-stakes domains that heavily hinge on such interpretability claims. Building on prior work, we make three proposals: (i) avoid treating CoT as being sufficient for interpretability without additional verification, (ii) adopt rigorous methods that assess faithfulness for downstream decision-making, and (iii) report such assessments alongside any interpretability claims based on CoT, while continuing to use CoT for its communicative and monitoring benefits.

title: Barrier-Based Safety Filtering for Quadrotor Flight in Cluttered Environments Under Acceleration Limits
summary: Accurate trajectory tracking alone does not guarantee safe quadrotor flight when the reference passes near obstacles or the available control authority is limited. This paper presents a safety-filtered trajectory-tracking framework for a quadrotor operating at a fixed altitude in obstacle-cluttered environments. A nominal tracking controller is combined with high-order control barrier constraints and an acceleration-constrained quadratic program. The safety filter preserves the nominal acceleration whenever it is admissible and modifies it only when the prescribed obstacle clearance is threatened. The analysis establishes nominal exponential tracking, forward invariance of the safe region under compatible initial conditions and continued quadratic-program feasibility, and bounded tracking error during safety intervention. Numerical experiments using an idealized planar translational model with single and multiple stationary circular obstacles show minimum clearances of $0.000$--$0.001$~m under the safety filter, compared with $-1.594/-1.421$~m under nominal control. Tracking RMSE increases from $0.618$ to $0.950$~m across reference-speed scales $0.6$--$1.6$, illustrating the effect of reference speed on tracking accuracy under safety constraints. Additional tests examine how acceleration limits affect control effort and feasibility. These findings inform safety-filter design for UAV trajectory tracking under limited control authority.

title: Model Order Detection with Parameter Estimation Guarantees for the Matrix Pencil Method
summary: Detecting the model order and estimating the parameters of sums of damped complex exponentials in noise is challenging when poles are closely spaced, the sample size is small, or the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) is low. We propose REECAP, a matrix pencil (MP) algorithm for joint model order detection and pole estimation. The algorithm computes candidate poles using an overestimated working rank and classifies them using a score derived from their associated eigenvectors. The model order is then estimated by counting the retained candidates. The score measures the eigenvector energy concentration in coordinates corresponding to the dominant right singular subspace of the data Hankel matrix. Under a suitable rank condition, we derive a deterministic sufficient condition guaranteeing that a candidate whose score exceeds a certain threshold lies within a prescribed tolerance of at least one signal pole. This establishes a theoretical connection between eigenvector energy concentration and pole-estimation accuracy. Extensive simulations demonstrate improved model order detection and frequency estimation performance relative to conventional MP order detection methods, recent structure-aware MP methods, and information-theoretic criteria (ITC), across a broad range of scenarios, including clustered frequencies, low SNR in the threshold region, and small sample sizes. Runtime comparisons further demonstrate substantial computational savings, and moderate sensitivity to noise model mismatch, compared to the evaluated structure-aware and information-theoretic methods.

title: Ternary Perfect $2$-Burst-Correcting Codes
summary: A construction for a ternary perfect linear $2$-burst-correcting code is presented for every redundancy $r \geq 5$. The construction is recursive with seeds given for $5 \leq r \leq 7$. The construction of redundancy $r \geq 8$ is derived from a code of redundancy $r-3$ and it distinguishes between codes of even and odd length.

title: Operationalizing Quantum Machine Learning for IoT Network Intrusion Detection
summary: The rapid growth of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased networked systems' exposure to cyber threats, making Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) essential for securing heterogeneous environments. While Deep Learning (DL) has shown strong performance in traffic analysis, Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has recently gained attention as an alternative approach to learn complex traffic patterns. We assess QML's practical applicability to intrusion detection in heterogeneous IoT scenarios. We present a hybrid quantum-classical NIDS and evaluate it on three recent IoT security datasets, under operationally relevant conditions. Beyond detection accuracy, we compare QML with a classical DL baseline across five operational perspectives: (i) performance under data scarcity, (ii) transferability through cross-domain evaluation, (iii) resilience to temporal constraints, (iv) robustness to quantum non-idealities across multiple noisy backends, and (v) prediction trustworthiness through calibration analysis. Experiments on binary and multiclass misuse detection show that DL generally outperforms QML under ideal and noisy conditions. However, QML remains competitive in data-scarcity and domain-shift scenarios and can outperform the DL baseline under temporal constraints.

title: Scoring Recovery-Time Agent Security: Proposals, Effects, and Retry Instructions
comment: 19 pages, 3 figures, 13 tables; 5,040 API episodes plus 720 separately configured Claude Code episodes, including 432 three-model calibration episodes; bounded protocol checks
summary: A timed-out tool write may be absent, committed, or still in flight. Evaluating an agent only on whether its goal exists can hide harmful recovery actions: auditing 12 supplied traces changes apparent completion from 10/12 to 8/12. We introduce an executable evaluation that separately records tool proposals, runtime decisions, and committed effects. In 3,456 model episodes, the original task wording produces only 39/576 valid recoveries when the initial write is absent; a combined clarification produces 576/576. A further 1,584 episodes test stronger attacks and separate the effect definition from the recovery recipe with three rollouts per absent-state cell. Definition alone yields 276/288 valid recoveries; recipe alone yields 288/288. For Luna, malicious text is associated with 11.1 percentage points fewer valid recoveries under both original and definition-only wording, an availability signal limited by shared tasks and templates. The stronger attacks produce no attempted unauthorized or changed-key action and no unsafe effect. A trajectory audit finds six original-key retries after observing pending status: five denied and one deduplicated. Bounded checks distinguish atomic key enforcement from a delayed-commit race; stale negative reads also invalidate the evidence gate. A separate Claude Code program adds 720 successful episodes: 288 under the original attacks and 432 stronger-attack calibration episodes across Opus, Sonnet, and Haiku 5.5, with no observed proposal or effect deviations. The contribution is a measurement design and a diagnosis of availability, specification, and contract sensitivity, with no demonstrated general defense efficacy.

title: Hidden Clues in WM-811K: Uncovering the Spatial Signals Behind Wafer Map Prediction
summary: WM-811K (also known as LSWMD) is a wafer map dataset first made publicly available in a 2015 paper by Wu et al. Convolutional neural networks have been used to achieve high classification accuracy on this dataset, yet it's not easy to decipher which features of the dataset are driving that performance. This study attempts to answer this specifically for WM-811K: how much of the predictive performance results from the wafer layout, the count of failed dies, their distance from the center and their exact 2-D location. After analyzing duplicate wafer maps, removing same wafer maps with conflicting labels and ensuring that the same manufacturing lot or exact same map doesn't appear in training, validation and test data, we were left with 25,513 defect-labeled wafer maps from eight classes. We then constructed four variations of each wafer map. The Original was the actual wafer map present in the dataset. The Layout-only kept only the layout of the non-background dies. The Global-shuffle kept the count of failed dies while shuffling them around. The Radial-shuffle randomized the locations of failed dies only in their radial bin, which was chosen out of 8 radial bins based on distance from the center. The data split, preprocessing and CNN architecture remained the same for all four of them. Macro-F1 progressed like this: 0.3829 (Layout-only), 0.5803 (Global-shuffle), 0.7439 (Radial-shuffle) and 0.8563 (Original). These results show that WM-811K contains useful information at several levels: wafer layout, number of failures, distribution of failed dies in a given radius, and exact 2-D locations of the failed dies. Therefore, high classification performance on this benchmark does not come only from learning the exact defect configuration.

title: Active road noise control using networked mean-square learning and lightweight conditional compensation experts
summary: Multichannel active road noise control (ARNC) requires effective noise reduction (NR) under causality and computational constraints. A computationally efficient method is proposed that separates linear control from condition-dependent nonlinear residual compensation. A finite impulse response (FIR) baseline filter is obtained through networked mean-square learning that can be made adaptive, while a multi-resolution FIR mixture-of-experts (MRF-MoE) module provides possibly nonlinear corrections. Training comprises baseline initialization, sample-graph-regularized expert and router optimization, and joint refinement. Target channels are treated as nodes in a connected network for mean-square error minimization, whereas training windows define a graph for regularizing routing probabilities. Each expert combines short-time dense and long-tail low-rank FIR filtering, and causal single-expert routing reduces inference computation. Compared with WaveNet-VNN under the same configuration, the proposed method reduces estimated inference cost by 96.3% while achieving higher NR on the test set.

title: EEGJev: A System One Decision Model and Benchmark for Multi-Task EEG Question Answering
summary: A single electroencephalographic (EEG) recording can support multiple decoding tasks. Fixed-label tests cannot show how EEG foundation models handle changing questions or options. We introduce EEGJev, a fast decision model that scores candidate answers in one pass. Our benchmark, EEGJev-Bench, covers six question types across 19 public EEG sources. We held the recording and options fixed while switching between questions about attributes paired during training, such as facial expression and the hand participants were asked to use. Across 13 test sources, EEGJev selected a label for the requested attribute with 99.70% accuracy (49.20% under uniform choice). Balanced accuracy for the specific answer was 62.04%. Its 95th-percentile response time was shorter than NeuroLM's on matched validation questions answered individually. EEGJev lets users switch decoding targets by changing the question. With EEGJev-Bench, researchers can test whether new decoders follow the question more reliably, identify the correct answer more often, or both.

title: Joint Trajectory and Power Optimization for Movable-Antenna-Aided Secure Transmission
summary: This paper investigates joint trajectory and power optimization for movable antenna (MA)-aided secure transmission, where the MA can transmit during its movement. Specifically, the average secrecy rate is maximized subject to movement and power constraints, which couple the MA positions and transmit powers over time, respectively. To tackle this nonconvex problem, we first decouple the transmit powers via Lagrangian duality, where the optimal power for a given trajectory is derived in semi-closed form and shown to depend only on the current MA position. Accordingly, we decouple the MA positions by equivalently reformulating the problem on a discretized linear rail in terms of the farthest grid point and the number of time slots spent at each grid point. Then, from strong duality of the convex relaxation for each farthest point, we construct an asymptotically optimal solution in which the MA dwells at no more than two positions. Finally, a low-complexity dual-based branch-and-bound algorithm is developed to select the farthest grid point and certify the optimality gap. Simulation results show that the proposed design outperforms the benchmark schemes.

title: Gamification in the age of AI: surveying player perceptions of motivation, manipulation, and data protection
summary: Modern games and applications increasingly employ artificial intelligence (AI), user modeling, and gamification to influence user behavior, sustain engagement, and monetize attention. Although these mechanisms can enhance motivation and enjoyment, they also raise concerns about manipulation, personal data usage, and transparency. To examine how players perceive these dynamics, we conducted a survey with 28 adult participants. Respondents expressed strong concerns about the collection and exploitation of personal information in games and gamified applications, while also reporting low awareness and a limited sense of control over how their data is used. They evaluated progression features such as leveling systems and leaderboards as motivating. In contrast, they rated retention-focused mechanics such as daily login rewards and random reward reveals as highly manipulative. Participants reported that these systems can create fear of missing out or resemble gambling. Participants also expressed support for regulatory measures that limit exploitative design and protect vulnerable users. These findings reveal a clear gap between increasingly powerful engagement strategies and user trust, illustrating the need for more responsible and transparent gamification practices.

title: Trustworthy Edge AI: Security, Privacy, and Resilience for Distributed Intelligence
comment: This the preprint of the chapter which has been accpeted for publication in the book titled "Edge AI Principles, Technologies and Applications", Wiley IEEE Press, edited by Qusay Fadhel. The chapter has 46 pages, and it contains 6 tables and 6 figures
summary: This chapter examines the principles and emerging research directions for building secure, privacy-preserving, and resilient Edge Artificial Intelligence (Edge AI) systems. As intelligence shifts from centralized clouds to distributed edge environments, challenges arise in ensuring data integrity, privacy, and reliable operation under adversarial and uncertain conditions. The chapter analyzes Edge AI architectures, emphasizing the expanded attack surface due to heterogeneous devices, resource constraints, and dynamic networks. It reviews core security mechanisms, including hardware-rooted trust, zero-trust models, secure communication, and attestation. Privacy-preserving approaches, such as federated learning, secure aggregation, and differential privacy, enable collaborative intelligence without centralized data sharing. Resilience strategies, including fault tolerance, adversarial robustness, and adaptive orchestration, are also explored. Case studies from smart cities, autonomous vehicles, healthcare, and industrial IoT illustrate practical trade-offs. The chapter advocates a holistic, cross-layer design integrating security, privacy, and resilience for trustworthy edge intelligence.

title: Conformalized Tree-Based Gradient Ensembles for Out-of-Distribution Detection and Plausible Recourse
summary: Counterfactual recourse provides actionable feature adjustments that reverse unfavourable predictions made by automated decision models. However, when recourse search optimizes purely against classifier confidence or narrow proxy scores over gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDT), search procedures can exploit boundary artifacts and low-density regions---an instance of Goodhart's law---yielding out-of-distribution (OOD) recommendations that appear favourable nominally while lacking manifold plausibility. In this paper, we study conformalized OOD gating coupled with actionability-constrained counterfactual search across two tabular benchmarks: Adult and Give Me Some Credit (GMSC). Calibrating finite-sample anomaly gates (gate_IF, gate_LOF, and the conjunctive gate_ALL) at significance level delta = 0.05 over isolation forest, local outlier factor, and k-nearest-neighbor signals, we audit generated counterfactuals against held-out GMM and OCSVM detectors alongside ablation studies (gen10, gen100, and relax). Across matched recourse pairs where both constrained and unconstrained searches succeed, gate_ALL significantly reduces held-out OCSVM flags on Adult (N=541, Delta flag_OCSVM = -0.0296, p_Holm = 4.0e-4) and lowers both held-out flags on GMSC (N=540, Delta flag_OCSVM = -0.0346, p = 1.0751e-4; Delta flag_GMM = -0.1663, p = 3.5679e-16) while increasing matched recourse cost (Delta cost = +0.3035, p = 1.3365e-5) and narrowing overall feasibility. Our findings formalize the cost--feasibility--plausibility trade-off and demonstrate how conformal OOD gating audits recourse reliability on tabular ensembles.

title: Iterative Identification of Aperiodic Sampled-Data Systems via Affine LPV Models Scheduled by the Sampling Interval
summary: This paper proposes a method for identifying a control-oriented model of a stable continuous-time linear system from aperiodically sampled input-output data. Rather than recovering the continuous-time matrices, the method directly identifies a discrete-time linear parameter-varying (LPV) state-space model that depends affinely on the measured normalized sampling-interval variation, a structure obtained from the first-order expansion of the zero-order-hold discretization. The resulting model is directly usable in control design for aperiodic sampled-data systems. An initial LPV estimate, including approximate first-order terms, is derived from a standard LTI subspace model through sampled-data relations. The method then iteratively alternates state-sequence reconstruction and LPV parameter refitting. Numerical examples show that the identified model retains high validation accuracy over a wide range of sampling-interval variations where a fixed LTI model degrades. Already at initialization, the state-space LPV structure substantially outperforms an LPV-ARX regression with the same scheduling variable, and the iterative refinement brings the model close to a state-measured benchmark, a practical upper-bound reference.

title: Wireless-OptSG: A Versatile Multi-Agent Optimization Framework for Wireless Resource Allocation
summary: 6G wireless networks are expected to accommodate heterogeneous service requirements across diverse deployment scenarios, giving rise to physical-layer resource allocation problems with scenario-dependent objectives and constraints. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agent systems can interpret wireless-domain specifications and incorporate execution feedback into optimization. However, translating language-level reasoning into feasible, high-quality resource allocations remains challenging, since candidates need to satisfy precise mathematical constraints throughout iterative search. This work proposes the Wireless Optimization Solution Generator (Wireless-OptSG), a versatile multi-agent framework for physical-layer resource allocation. Wireless-OptSG organizes optimization as a feedback-driven candidate search guided by a static meta-prompt and an evolving optimization history. In a nested outer-inner loop, parallel agents explore solution trajectories and periodically exchange high-quality records to guide candidate generation. Feasible initialization uses executable optimization primitives, while a tiered repair pipeline restores feasibility and solution-dependent context improves retained-record informativeness. Experiments on four representative tasks under perfect and imperfect channel state information show that Wireless-OptSG achieves performance comparable to scenario-specific state-of-the-art (SOTA) solvers, exceeds SOTA in some settings, and consistently outperforms generic baselines, demonstrating its potential as a transferable optimization framework for future wireless networks.

title: Multi-User Linear Precoder Optimization for Obfuscation-Aided Mixed Regular and Wiretap Coding
comment: 6 pages + 7 pages appendix, 6 figures, 3 tables, 1 algorithm. Extended version of the manuscript submitted to IEEE WCNC 2027, including the detailed derivation of the SCA algorithm
summary: Physical-layer security has attracted considerable research interest with the development of quantum computing. One prominent approach is wiretap coding, which exploits the channel advantage of a legitimate receiver over an eavesdropper to achieve secure communication. However, under unfavorable channel conditions, wiretap coding can significantly reduce the achievable rate compared to regular channel coding. Mixed coding alleviates this limitation by using wiretap coding to protect a short secret required for obfuscation, while the obfuscated payload is encoded using regular channel coding. In this work, we propose a generalized obfuscation-aided mixed-coding system based on the multi-user (MU)-linear precoding (LP) architecture that unifies existing approaches employing different obfuscation functions. We then formulate the corresponding precoder optimization problem, abstracting the obfuscation function through a minimum secrecy rate constraint. Numerical simulations using a geometric two-user line-of-sight (LoS) channel demonstrated how the minimum secrecy rate requirement determines the operating point of mixed coding between regular and wiretap coding. Subsequent beampattern analysis revealed a key synergy between mixed coding and precoding: Mixed coding enables individual beam shaping for the two coding layers. Finally, spatial analysis showed that mixed coding offers the largest sum-rate gains when users are positioned at similar angles.

title: Quantum Switches Under Congestion: Stabilization, Scheduling, and Performance
summary: Quantum Communications (QC) are set to revolutionize communications by employing and exploiting the properties of quantum systems. In this work, we analyse Quantum Switch Networks (QSN) comprised of quantum switches, both memory-equipped and all-optical switch types, to study the time evolution of the requests' queue lengths and how they behave under certain regimes given by various configurations of the network, all governed by the throughput-optimal, classical MaxWeight Scheduling Policy. The goals of this work are twofold: first, we study the queue length dynamics, evolution and equilibrium under the Fluid Queues Approximation model and as a discrete evolution problem, with the addition of a simple discarding policy that stabilizes any scheduling policy by the introduction of a friction-like term named \textit{discard term} inside the evolution equations. The second goal is the validation of the mechanism by comparing the discrete queue evolution of all-optical and memory-equipped quantum networks under different constraints and complex topologies like BCube and Fat-Tree, which are key topologies present on future Quantum Data Centres.

title: High Throughput Meets Low Latency: CKKS Functional Bootstrapping on GPUs
summary: Functional (programmable) bootstrapping extends the bootstrapping operation of Fully Homomorphic Encryption (FHE) to evaluate an arbitrary function while refreshing a ciphertext. This capability was a unique feature of scalar CGGI/DM cryptosystems for many years until it was recently added to the toolset of vectorized FHE schemes, with CKKS being the most promising option both in terms of throughput (amortized time) and functionality. Previous work showed that CKKS functional bootstrapping outperforms CGGI/DM functional bootstrapping in terms of throughput by two to three orders of magnitude, but still loses in latency on CPU by two to three orders of magnitude. We present an optimized GPU implementation of CKKS functional bootstrapping that closes the latency gap. Our implementation supports evaluating functions over both small integers (as in CGGI/DM) and real numbers (unique to CKKS), which we call discrete-CKKS and continuous-CKKS functional bootstrapping, respectively.

title: Layer-Readout Interfaces in EEG Foundation Models: Predictive Accessibility and Cross-Dataset Transfer
summary: Intermediate layers often outperform final layers when foundation models are used as frozen feature extractors, but the source of this advantage is unclear. We study this question in EEG foundation models by separating three factors: how representations are read out, whether intermediate layers provide predictive utility beyond the final-layer interface, and whether useful depth structure transfers across datasets. Across five models and three tasks, improving the final-layer readout consistently recovers substantial predictive performance, yet intermediate layers remain advantageous within frozen extraction. We also find that layers selected on one dataset remain useful on another across five dataset pairs and four task families, and that a compact set of source-derived task directions retains predictive value after transfer in sleep staging. Together, these results show that predictive utility varies across depth, and its usefulness depends on how representations are read out and transferred. More crucially, source-selected layers provide a reusable feature interface across datasets, reducing the need for target-side layer search while outperforming final-layer baselines on target datasets.

title: Damping Ratio and Convergence Rate Analysis for Inverter-Based Power Systems via Root Locus
comment: This manuscript has been accepted by IFAC 2026
summary: As more renewables enter the grid, it becomes insufficient to rely solely on the center of inertia frequency to analyze the transient performance, especially for oscillation behaviors. Motivated by this, we study the transient frequency performance of inverter-based power systems. Two key performance criteria are considered: the damping ratio and the convergence rate, which are determined by the angles and the real parts of the closed-loop poles, respectively. By decomposing the network system into a set of scalar feedback systems, we show that the closed-loop poles can be analyzed using the root locus of a scalar feedback system as the gain varies from the smallest nonzero eigenvalue to the largest eigenvalue of the scaled Laplacian matrix of the interconnection network. Based on this, we derive sufficient conditions that ensure desired damping and convergence performance. Our analysis shows that the worst-case damping ratio and convergence rate occur when the gain equals the largest and the smallest nonzero eigenvalues of the scaled Laplacian, respectively. This result significantly simplifies the performance assessment. We further provide guidelines for tuning the inverter parameter. Numerical simulations are included to illustrate and validate the proposed approach.

title: Strategic Beam Brainstorming for Generative Site-Specific Beamforming
summary: A novel plug-and-play candidate beam selection strategy is proposed for generative site-specific beamforming (GenSSBF), a paradigm that draws on a learned conditional channel distribution to generate multiple plausible beams. Under a limited probing budget, realizing the full potential of GenSSBF requires identifying which candidate beams are worth probing. To this end, the marginal probing value is first derived to guide strategic candidate probing by quantifying each beam's additional gain beyond those already selected. Based on this criterion, two algorithms are developed without retraining the generator: 1) Greedy candidate probing (GCP) selects all candidate beams from a locally generated pool prior to over-the-air probing, requiring only a single feedback round; 2) Adaptive candidate probing (ACP) exploits reference signal received power (RSRP) feedback after each probe to update channel hypothesis weights and guide the next beam selection, without increasing the asymptotic complexity. Simulations across three ray-tracing scenarios under noiseless and noisy probing reveal that: 1) candidate complementarity is key to efficient beam brainstorming; and 2) ACP is particularly beneficial when initial sensing leaves substantial channel uncertainty and subsequent feedback is reliable.

title: Deterministic Polar Subcode Design via Exact Low-Weight Spectrum Characterization
summary: We develop a deterministic framework for improving polar-subcode minimum distance through information-set selection and dynamic frozen expression design. Expression design faces two difficulties. Changing an expression can introduce new low-weight codewords, and excluding different codewords can impose conflicting requirements on the same coefficients. To address both difficulties, we first fix the information set and release the editable frozen constraints to form a common supercode containing every candidate code. Its low-weight codewords give necessary and sufficient conditions for one coefficient assignment to exclude every codeword of the specified weights. To apply these conditions at longer lengths, we use the polar decomposition. At each split, a one in the left codeword gives two complementary output bits whose combined weight is always one. We can therefore eliminate the corresponding variables from the parity checks and count their compatible assignments to obtain the exact low-weight spectrum. With both constituent codes fixed, the same reduced checks also simplify the coefficient search. Assignments that give identical check values across all relevant messages share one representative, from which the entire group can be recovered. We give sufficient conditions for choosing the coefficients sequentially without backtracking. Finally, we use the outcome of expression design on one information set to guide exchanges of information positions for the next, linking the two design steps. In experiments spanning block lengths from 64 to 1024 and several code rates, the proposed design meets the target minimum distances in minutes and achieves competitive frame error rates under successive cancellation list decoding.

title: MAQR: Lightweight Memory-Aware Q-Routing for Fresh Status Delivery in Multi-Hop IoBNTs
summary: This paper proposes memory-aware Q-routing (MAQR) for fresh status delivery over history-dependent molecular links in multi-hop Internet of Bio-Nano Things (IoBNT) networks. Repeated transmissions leave residual molecules, making link reliability history-dependent and fixed routing inefficient. Each link is calibrated from a spatial Markov model and approximated by three nonnegative decay modes. The resulting reduced memory state and packet bit composition provide an instantaneous link-success estimate. MAQR combines quantized memory and reliability descriptors with packet age, queue occupancy, and molecule reserve in a lightweight partially observable Q-routing heuristic. It is trained offline and requires only reduced-state updates and Q-table lookup during deployment. Across five independent training pairs and 20 shared evaluation seeds, MAQR reduces mean AoI by 46.9 % relative to memory-blind Q-routing at 0.30 packets/slot while improving molecular efficiency. Frozen-policy sweeps further show comparable performance under weak memory and an increasing MAQR advantage as channel memory strengthens.

title: Per-Attack Blocking Hides Catalog Vulnerability: A Weakest-Link Analysis of Tool Manifests
comment: Accepted at the Third Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD), NeurIPS 2026. 17 pages, 3 figures
summary: Runtime controls for tool-using agents depend on manifests that state what each tool may read and where its output may go. Evaluations of these controls, including ChainCaps, report per-attack blocking: the share of attacks a set of manifests stops. We show that this is the wrong unit. A catalog is only as safe as its weakest source policy: if $M$ independently authored policies are each wrong with probability $p$, the chance that the catalog contains an accepted exfiltration path is $1-(1-p)^M$, while per-attack blocking stays at $1-p$. Three lines of evidence agree. In synthetic catalogs run through two enforcement engines, ChainCaps and OpenAPPA, per-attack blocking holds at 92% while catalog vulnerability rises from 22% at 10 tools to 99% at 200, and composition provides no protective effect. A fifteen-model authoring pilot shows that real errors cluster by author, so a 200-tool catalog behaves like about 5 independent decisions rather than 60 (95% interval 3.4 to 9.2). On 114 real MCP tools with expert-written rules, the models' own manifests block 89% of attacks yet leave 9 of 15 catalogs open, as the author-effect model predicts and independence does not. Evaluations should report catalog vulnerability, the sink coverage of their tests, and an effective number of independent decisions alongside per-attack blocking.

title: Flagging Batch Shift in Flow Cytometry using Jeffreys Divergence between Gaussian Mixtures
summary: Machine learning models for clinical flow cytometry are usually evaluated on data drawn from their training distribution. In routine practice, however, acquisition conditions and reagents may change, potentially making predictions unreliable without warning. We propose a model agnostic criterion for prediction reliability based on a notion of distance from the training distribution: each patient sample is represented by a Gaussian mixture model, and its Jeffreys divergence to a reference fitted on the training data is estimated using Monte Carlo integration. We illustrate our approach on real-life shifted cohorts of acute myeloid leukaemia patients, using a classifier trained to predict NPM1 mutation status. First, we show graphically and statistically that pairwise divergences capture acquisition cohort structure. We then calibrate a rejection threshold on a subset of shifted cohort samples and evaluate it on held-out subjects. Across 20 runs, the misclassification rate of rejected samples was 2.5 times larger than for retained samples. These results suggest that input divergence can help identify unreliable predictions, providing a strong candidate component for abstention frameworks, along with quality control measures and classifier confidence.

title: Online outlier-resilient data-driven moving horizon estimation for linear discrete-time systems
summary: This paper addresses data-driven state estimation for linear systems of which online output measurements may be corrupted by sparse outliers of arbitrary magnitude. Using only offline input-state-output data without explicitly identifying a system model, we propose an outlier-resilient data-driven moving horizon estimation scheme, termed OORD-MHE, based on Willems' fundamental lemma. The scheme employs a truncated-quadratic loss on the output residuals, parameterized by a truncation threshold, to mitigate the influence of online outliers. We establish sufficient conditions under which the resulting estimation error remains uniformly bounded. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed OORD-MHE scheme generates accurate state estimates in the presence of sparse online outliers.

title: Net-Gain-Optimized Constellation Shaping for the 5G NR DFT-s-OFDM Uplink: Probabilistic, Geometric, and Joint Designs
summary: Constellation shaping improves the achievable information rate of coded modulation. On the single-carrier uplink waveform of 5G New Radio, discrete Fourier transform (DFT)- spread orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM), the same shaping can also raise the peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR). A higher PAPR forces more power amplifier back- off and reduces the link budget. Prior work characterized this penalty for fixed probabilistically and geometrically shaped constellations, but did not turn the trade-off into a design objective. We optimize constellation shaping (CS) to maximize the net-gain, i.e., the sum of the communication gain and the PAPR gain, at the fixed spectral efficiency of 4 bits per channel use for 64-QAM. We apply it to probabilistic shaping (PS), geometric shaping (GS), and a joint scheme that combines both. As the coded block error rate cannot be evaluated inside a gradient loop, we use the achievable information rate as a surrogate for the communication performance and the PAPR surrogate as differentiable cost functions for the optimizer. The learned constellations are then validated on a complete DFT-s-OFDM link-level chain. Conventional Maxwell-Boltzmann PS yields a negative net-gain, but net-gain-aware optimization removes this deficit in every method. GS converts it into a substantial gain, as it not only improves the communication performance but also lowers the PAPR below the uniform 64-QAM reference, achieving the largest net-gain among the CS methods studied.

title: Explicit Constructions of MDS Cyclic Codes from Rational Function Fields
summary: We present a unified construction of maximum distance separable (MDS) cyclic codes over \(\mathbb F_q\) from rational function fields. The evaluation places form a single orbit under a cyclic automorphism group, and the defining divisor is invariant under that group. We recover the classical existence results for lengths \(n\) satisfying \(n\mid(q-1)\), \(n=p\), or \(n\mid(q+1)\), where \(p=\operatorname{char}(\mathbb F_q)\). For odd divisors \(n\) of \(q+1\), we construct codes in every even dimension \(2\leq k\leq n-1\) using a second orbit of rational places for \(n<q+1\) and duality for \(n=q+1\). Finally, we use the repeated-root factorization of \(x^n-1\) to give a direct proof of the classical result that no nontrivial MDS cyclic code of length \(n\) exists when \(p\mid n\) and \(n\ne p\).

title: FugaStream: Pipelined Live Volumetric Streaming towards Full Exploitation of Multi-views
summary: Live volumetric streaming has become the cornerstone of next-generation immersive applications, enabling users to experience six degrees of freedom (6-DoF). To support interactivity, live volumetric streaming must reconstruct multi-view RGB-D frames into a unified 3D representation while meeting a stringent latency budget, where existing systems are forced to trade reconstruction quality for latency. In this paper, we present FugaStream, the first pipelined live volumetric streaming system that mitigates this trade-off by committing a base representation early and then incrementally merging novel late views. Enabling such functionalities introduces two fundamental challenges: (i) the uncertainty in frame availability, and (ii) the late view updates in a lightweight manner. We address these challenges through two key algorithms: (i) adaptive base commitment control, which determines the base commitment time with the expected reconstruction gain of each missing view against the growing cost of latency, and (ii) base-referenced late view completion, which transmits only the novel regions of late views compared to early committed base, enabling lightweight fusion at the client. We validate the effectiveness of FugaStream on a widely used volumetric dataset and a real-world testbed, demonstrating that FugaStream improves SSIM by 10.9% and IoU by 13.7% over baselines under the same 150 ms budget.

title: Leaks by Installments: Cross-Session Answer Disclosure in LLM Tutors and a Ledger-Based Defense
summary: Tutors built on large language models (LLMs) are told not to give away answers, but a learner does not have to ask for the answer all at once. Existing safeguards judge each reply within the current conversation, so a learner can open a new session, reword the problem, or request a worked solution to the same problem with different numbers. We call this cross-session disclosure and propose a defense: a persistent, per-learner disclosure ledger. For every problem a learner brings, the system builds a typed solution graph. Before a reply is released, a gate matches the reply's own content, not the learner's wording, against the ledger by result values and by type-labeled solution structure, then computes which steps the learner could now derive. The reply is withheld if that set reaches the final answer or exceeds a budget. In a simulation of 3,000 problems, the ledger reduced leakage through renumbered practice variants from 100% to 10.6% while honest learners completed 94-99.5% of problems. With two real LLM tutors (Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct and Phi-3.5-mini-instruct) on 60 problems, leakage through renumbered variants fell from 0.58 to 0.08 and from 1.00 to 0.18, with 98% honest completion. The ledger did not reduce split requests beyond a per-session gate in the live runs. All acceptance criteria were fixed before each run.

title: Fusion Gains Depend on the Implementation and the Calibration Target: An 18-Task Study of Prediction Intervals with a Single-Source Fallback
comment: 4 figures; supplementary material included as an ancillary file
summary: A fused model can benefit from an extra learning stage as well as from a second data source. We compare four fusion implementations with matched single-source learners on 18 regression tasks with prediction intervals. Across ten refits under group-wise calibration, linear stacking improved the interval score by 6.0% against a source model without a second stage and by 0.1% against its matched single source. The four implementations agreed on 3 of 18 tasks and gave opposite clear verdicts on 12, including 8 of the 10 tasks with naturally distinct sources. With pointwise calibration, they agreed on 5 tasks and gave opposite clear verdicts on 9. A development-set selector with a matched single-source fallback improved ten-refit task-averaged scores by 2.2--6.3% in every implementation under both calibrations. Adding fused arms to the pool of single-source candidates improved the mean relative score by about 5 percentage points. Under group-wise calibration, the gradient-boosted selector met the criterion frozen before evaluation on eight held-out tasks. In post-opening refits, selectors lost to the matched single source in 4.4--6.1% of task-level runs under group-wise calibration. Under signed pointwise calibration, three implementations lost in 19--23% of runs. Fusion evaluations should compare matched candidates on held-out data and report how often the selector loses alongside its average gain.

title: Stability and periodic switching in feedback systems with sector-bounded hybrid integrators
summary: We study stability of piecewise linear systems composed of the feedback interconnection of a linear time-invariant process and a sector-bounded hybrid integrator. Exploiting the observation that for such systems state-dependent switching sequences asymptotically exhibit periodic behaviour, we develop a spectral approach to stability analysis as an alternative to sufficient Lyapunov-based methods. We formulate a conjecture that asymptotic periodicity holds irrespective of the initial conditions and system stability, and provide a description of the limit system and propose an algorithm to obtain its parameters. We establish this rigorously for second-order linear-time invariant processes. Based on spectral properties of the resulting periodic limit system, we derive sufficient stability conditions. The results provide a novel viewpoint for accurate stability analysis of general state-based piecewise linear systems.

title: CRISP: Sparse Risk-Calibrated Front-End Allocation and Fusion for Low-Resolution Snapshot GNSS Positioning
summary: Low-resolution global navigation satellite system snapshot receivers face strong coupling among automatic gain control compression, coarse quantization, and waveform distortion from nonlinear interference mitigation. This paper presents Cross-Risk Interference-Resilient Snapshot Positioning, denoted CRISP, an aided single-snapshot architecture that allocates and fuses complementary pre-correlation processors over a bounded position-clock search region under a shared direct position estimation solve budget. On a pre-frozen baseband descriptor partition, offline calibration estimates uncentered second-order position-error cross moments and solves cardinality-constrained simplex programs along east, north, and up axes, retaining validation-screened multibranch combinations while assigning single matched processors elsewhere. An online reliability gate screens the same quantized snapshot to route unfamiliar waveforms toward single-branch protective operators. We characterize profiled contrast shifts after nonlinear suppression and derive a conditional finite-sample excess-risk bound across disjoint splits alongside an exact same-snapshot gating risk identity. Across 17 568 simulated 2-ms GPS L1 C/A trials, CRISP reduces core positioning root-mean-square error by 13.84%, > 100-m gross errors by 41.32%, and multi-geometry error by 12.23% over Snapshot-FD at 1.43 core and 1.51 overall solves per snapshot.

title: Self-Orthogonal Minimal Codes from n-to-1 Mappings
summary: Self-orthogonal codes are central to the construction of quantum error-correcting codes, and minimal codes yield secret-sharing schemes whose access structures are read off from the supports of their codewords. A code that is both self-orthogonal and minimal therefore serves both purposes at once, so that a single family of codes can produce a quantum code and a secret-sharing scheme simultaneously. Linear codes arising from n-to-1 mappings over finite fields are a natural source of such codes and have attracted considerable attention recently, yet their parameters and weight distributions remain difficult to determine: for most high-degree functions the Walsh spectra cannot be computed directly, and it is precisely these weights on which the analysis of minimality and self-orthogonality rests. We address this difficulty through the algebraic theory of skew polynomial rings. Using the right greatest common divisor of skew polynomials, we determine the dimensions of the kernel spaces of the linearized polynomials associated with the n-to-1 mappings, which in turn yield the weight distributions of the corresponding codes. With this method we treat two newly constructed families of n-to-1 functions together with one known family, and obtain the exact weight distributions of the resulting codes; we further prove that all of these codes are minimal and self-orthogonal. Each family therefore simultaneously yields a quantum error-correcting code and a secret-sharing scheme, with explicitly determined parameters and access structures. This work offers a new perspective for determining the parameters of linear codes derived from n-to-1 mappings.

title: Quantization-Induced Performance Degradation in Segment Routing: A Concentration Inequality Analysis
summary: In segment routing (SR), splitting ratios must be quantized to respect practical hardware precision constraints. Yet no existing work has established an upper bound on the performance degradation caused by such quantization. In this work, we propose source-agnostic systematic rounding, which allows flows sharing a destination to share the same policy, thereby reducing memory consumption, and which approximates the target splitting ratios by a set of power-of-two terms so as to respect the hardware precision limit. We explicitly analyze the consequence of quantizing splitting ratios to integer multiples of 1/64 by a probability-theoretic argument based on concentration inequalities, and we derive an upper bound on the resulting performance degradation. We validate our analysis with extensive experiments on real-world network topologies and flow statistics.

title: The Fingerprinting Paradox: Why Sensitivity Undermines Black-Box Model Integrity Verification
summary: Black-box integrity verification aims to detect unauthorized modifications to outsourced models using only prediction APIs.
